cur:manuscripts-de-laudibus-bnf-lamb.summary: At the centre of a letter grid, the Lamb of God stands with a cross-nimbus, flanked by the lion and ox of the evangelists and with the eagle above and the man-angel below, each bearing a label; together they form the shape of a cross across the page. Christ appears here in symbolic form as the Lamb, proclaimed by the four Gospels.
facts: Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda and later Archbishop of Mainz, composed this cycle of figure-poems (carmina figurata) in praise of the Cross around 810; each page is a grid of letters in which shapes pick out further verses.
The figures are arranged at the ends and centre of an invisible cross, so that the whole grid again praises the Cross.
cur:manuscripts-de-laudibus-bnf-lamb.notes: Christ is represented symbolically as the Lamb. Poem number given according to the usual order of the cycle; not stated on the Commons file.

cur:manuscripts-egberti-wedding-cana.summary: Christ, labelled IHS XPS, stands at the right and gestures toward the stone jars, while the Virgin, labelled S(an)C(t)A MARIA, turns to him, and servants pour water into the vessels at the left. The words 'And when they wanted wine, the mother of Jesus saith unto him' run beneath the picture.
facts: The Codex Egberti, a Gospel lectionary made for Archbishop Egbert of Trier, is described as the oldest surviving New Testament picture cycle of the life of Christ in the Ottonian era: 52 of its 60 paintings illustrate Gospel readings in the order of the church year.
During the Second World War the codex was evacuated to Giessen University Library, survived its bombing in December 1944, and was brought back to Trier in May 1945 from a parsonage at Elkerhausen.

cur:monumental-san-vitale-lamb-of-god.summary: At the crown of the presbytery vault, a white haloed Lamb stands against a dark blue sky scattered with gold stars, enclosed in a wreath of leaves, fruit and flowers. The wreath is upheld by four angels standing on globes (not visible in this detail), so that the whole vault converges on Christ as the sacrificial Lamb directly above the altar.
facts: The cross-ribbed vault is covered with acanthus scrolls, birds and animals, all converging on the wreath that frames the Lamb.
Placing the Lamb above the altar linked the image to the Eucharist celebrated beneath it, a theme continued in the lunettes of Abel, Melchizedek and Abraham on the presbytery walls.

cur:objects-athlone-crucifixion-plaque.summary: Christ fills the centre of this gilt-bronze plaque, robed in a garment covered with spirals and interlace, his large head with wide-open eyes showing that he is alive upon the cross. Above his arms hover two angels, and below stand the lance-bearer and the sponge-bearer. Abstract Celtic ornament transforms the Crucifixion into a solemn, timeless image of Christ's victory.
facts: Wikipedia describes it as the earliest and largest (21 cm) of the eight surviving early medieval Irish crucifixion plaques, found in the 19th century in the churchyard of St John's near Rinnegan, Co. Roscommon.
Rivet holes show that it was originally attached to a larger wooden object such as a processional cross, book shrine or altarpiece.
